Mr. Speaker, I cannot go any further, except once again to say that by following this course of adhering strictly to your reasoning and ruling places us in no other position than to vote blindly yes or no on each bill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was in the house on the November 15 when discussions took place about this matter. As I understood the proposition at that time, you attempted to indicate what the principle of the bill was, namely the relief to be provided to such-and-such a person, consisting of the dissolution of their marriage. I think the suggestion was made, or so I understood from the comments both of yourself and the hon. member, that one might look at the evidence taken in the other place in order to obtain information on the question whether or not there had been a marriage. If there had not been a marriage, of course there could be no relief granted; but I do not think it was ever suggested, and I certainly did not get this impression, that we should survey the sufficiency of the evidence and examine whether there was adequate evidence for the purpose. If the evidence taken in the other place was plainly and specifically directed to establishing that there was no marriage, then I think any hon. member could say that he objected and intended to vote against the principle of the bill, because there was no marriage and no relief to be given.
That is an altogether different position from suggesting, as does the hon. member for Skeena, that this gives him or any other hon. member the right carte blanche, to examine piece by piece and item by item the evidence taken before the committee of the other place so that in considering the principle of the bill on second reading, we could decide whether or not relief should be granted on the evidence taken before the divorce committee of the other place. If there was no evidence at all to establish the marriage, then I think that is adequate evidence on which to say that we are opposed to the bill; but we should not go into the sufficiency of the evidence, which is a different matter.

Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member who is opposing second reading of the bill, having based himself on some examples

he gave to the house, is confusing two things. When we have before the house a bill to change the name of a company-Allstate or any other-that is one matter. But these bills have all been before another committee. That committee has heard all the evidence. It has gone into all the proof which is available to this House of Commons, and the bills are now before us with all that evidence accepted and approved.
Mr. Speaker, I think on the date that the hon. member referred to I raised this question on a point of order, and Your Honour ruled upon it. Because you were generous enough to allow the hon. member to proceed a certain distance and ask certain questions or read certain evidence, I do not think it sets a binding precedent. We raised an objection then and you ruled upon it. We respectfully submit that what the hon. member is trying to do now is something altogether different from the examples he gave in dealing with an insurance company. These bills are before the house complete in all detail, and you are right, Mr. Speaker, when you say that all we can do now is to deal with the principle whether there should be an annulment or a dissolution of the marriage or whether there should not. As you have cited quite properly, I do not think we are in a position to go into all the evidence, as the hon. member suggests. If he wants to go into all the evidence for the sake of giving this house a lot of information it really does not need, and which it already has anyway in print, then I think he is completely out of order.

Mr. Speaker, I was very impressed, as I nearly always am, by what was said by the hon. member for Peace River. It seems to me that the point that the hon. gentleman made could very well be illustrated by this bill concerning the Merit Insurance Company. When we were discussing that matter I noticed that the hon. member for Skeena did not get up and ask whether there was a Merit Insurance Company, and ask for its marriage or its birth certificate. But it does not seem to me that it is reasonable or right, when all we are considering is the principle of a bill, for any hon. member to seek to transgress the rules of the house, or to take up the time

of the house which is supposed to be devoted exclusively to discussing the principle of this bill-and the only principle I can see is whether or not there should be a dissolution -by all sorts of irrelevaneies which are obviously not pertinent to the main question.

We want to avoid this whole impasse.

Well, speaking for myself, I say that I want to see parliament do what parliament ought to do, as long as there is no other method of doing it, and that is to provide relief in these cases.

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that if the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate had his way and the principle of this bill was that which he mentioned, namely whether we should handle these bills in the house or not, then that question would be debatable and a lot of people would co-operate with him. But it seems to me that in this as in the case of all other private bills there must be some principle or else we would not be handling it at all.
I find, not from looking at the evidence but from looking at the bill itself, that certain allegations are made, and some of those allegations must have some relationship to the principle. I think the allegations are the adultery charges and the other charges involved, which I think Your Honour has ruled are not to be discussed at this stage-and I think that is perfectly clear and correct. However, if there was no marriage of the parties described in this bill, then I think there is no principle, and unless the bill were worded differently there would be no point in its being before us.
For this reason I think we should have the opportunity, as we would with any other bill, of discussing that principle. Some hon. members may never have read one of these bills, and in case they have not, I should like to read not the preamble but one of the clauses to the bill. It says:
The said marriage is hereby dissolved and shall be henceforth null and void to all intents and purposes whatsoever.
Nothing can be amended or changed in any way if there is not a principle to change.

It would seem to me that the principle must be the marriage itself. I would respectfully submit, as the lawyers say, that this is the principle of this bill and that hon. members on second reading should concern themselves at least to this degree with the principle of the bill.

On two occasions in the last few minutes it has been said that we are limited to discussing the principle of the bill, that the principle of the bill is whether or not we wish to dissolve a marriage, that any member who wishes to object to the dissolution of a particular marriage can vote against the bill, and that those who wish to dissolve a marriage may vote for the bill. It seems to me that it is preposterous to ask me as a member of parliament to agree to the dissolution of a marriage or to vote against the dissolution of a marriage without being able to discuss and debate the alleged grounds for asking that the marriage be dissolved, without any opportunity to discuss whether or not proper and adequate provision has been made for the children of such a marriage, if there are any, and whether or not adequate provision has been made for the wife through alimony. How is any member of this House of Commons, intelligently and with a proper sense of responsibility, going to vote to dissolve a marriage unless the germane and relevant matters have been discussed and debated?
The hon. member referred to one marriage out of 500 that might come before parliament for investigation.

Not only with regard to one out of 500 but with regard to every one of the 500 I say you have the right to have this kind of information. If members of parliament are going to exercise the power to dissolve marriages, they ought to exercise it with a sense of responsibility. If ever there was a demonstration of the travesty of the House of Commons having this power, this is it. This is exactly why it ought to be taken away from this parliament. However, if we are to be compelled to exercise this power, then let us exercise it with a proper sense of responsibility. I submit that we cannot exercise it with a proper sense of responsibility unless we can discuss the grounds upon which it is wise and appropriate to dissolve a marriage or the grounds upon which we should vote against dissolving that marriage. I submit that I do not know how it is possible to discuss the principle of dissolving a marriage unless we can discuss and debate all the relevant facts which make it either advisable or inadvisable to grant dissolution of a marriage.

Since we are on an extremely important point of order, Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I might say a word in direct reply to what has been said by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. It seems to me that his argument, which would otherwise be valid, is based on a totally false premise. It seems to me that the false premise is that the agreement to the second reading would dissolve the marriage. It would do nothing of the kind. It would send the bill to a committee where any and every hon. member who wishes to do so can satisfy himself to his heart's content, in a proper atmosphere, where it could be done, not by debate and the clash of opinion but by the examination of evidence, something which cannot possibly be done on second reading in the House of Commons. If this were the only opportunity to consider the matter, if second reading in the house were the only opportunity to consider the merits of these cases, I would agree wholeheartedly with the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. However, it is not the only opportunity. All that second reading of this bill or of any other private bill is, is a device whereby this house gets it before a committee-as every private bill goes to a committee-where the evidence can be properly sifted. It is only on third reading that a decision is being made as to whether or not the bill shall pass and the relief be granted.
It therefore seems to me that the hon. gentleman's argument falls totally to the ground. All we are deciding really is whether there is a prima facie case for sending the bill on to the committee and nothing else. It seems to me that is the only thing that ought to be debated. To use the rules of the house as an indirect device, as some hon. members seem to wish to do, for seeking to impose the will of a minority upon the majority about a matter on which they cannot get the support of a majority, seems to me to be an abuse of the rules of the house.

I had not intended to speak on this bill, Mr. Speaker. I understand that this morning, as it has done on other occasions, the committee passed a block of nine or ten of the bills without calling a single witness and without doing anything but get the report from the other committee.

Atlantic Development Board or fears we have with regard to the proposed Atlantic development board, I would refer to one particular matter to which the minister, in introducing the resolution before us, referred-a matter he had also raised when he was premier of the province of New Brunswick-and that is that we hope that economic policies which would be adopted in relation to particular economic circumstances facing the nation as a whole would not be unilaterally applied to a particular region of the country such as the maritimes. This has, of course, particular significance in the situation such as that which faces Canada today. Because of the situation which exists, austerity is precisely that much more serious in our region. I was somewhat concerned at the reference the minister made, when he said something along these lines: that no preconceived suggestions or conclusions, would be acted upon. I can understand why he would want to refer to that, but once again I hope this is not a means of slowing down action which can be taken in certain fields by the government without further study.
We also hope that consideration will be given to the question of certain companies growing fat on government assistance. Because we are not demanding assistance for the sake of assistance. If there is a place for particular subsidies for a given industry, we would hope that these would be investigated and supervised in order that no particular section of our economy benefits as a result of the situation facing us in our area. Therefore I suggest that there are some major projects, such as the Chignecto canal, which I hope will not be proceeded with simply because some particular individual or some small group of individuals in the Atlantic provinces sees this type of project as something worth while. Perhaps it is; but I suggest that it is unlike those other conclusions we have reached in certain particular areas which we have been studying for a number of years, and on which there is agreement in the region and across the nation. This is a matter in relation to which we have to ask some questions, such as these: Who will benefit from a Chignecto canal project? Will it add in any considerable measure to the lives of our people in this region of Canada?
The minister, during the course of his introduction of this resolution, referred to the fact that for some reason or other we have lagged behind the rest of Canada. We understand what this reason is. In 1867 we decided to build and to found this nation of Canada. In order to do that we had to implement

and act upon national development policies- the trans-continental railway system, our tariff barriers, the opening of the west, and what have you. As a result of these policies, which were not based on traditional economic principles, we defied economics in order to build this nation, and in so doing we in the eastern region of Canada have suffered economically. Therefore we have reached a point where it is time that regional policies made up for the difficulties which have been created in our area while certain benefits were provided to people in other parts of Canada.
One final point, Mr. Chairman, with regard to any program of development in any region of Canada. I suggest that there is no hope in an Atlantic development board, or in any body involving a similar principle, for accomplishing the objectives of such a program until we can find the answer to solve the economic problems which face the nation. You cannot talk about full employment, which is a desirable goal for the Atlantic provinces, until we can provide full employment across Canada. We know what the situation has been over the years in that part of the country. We have witnessed and experienced some degree of prosperity when conditions were good in other parts of Canada, and the extra trickled over the brim and ran down to our people. The only times we have ever had real prosperity were during the railway construction boom and during the two previous world wars. We suggest that these are not events which are to be expected again soon, so that it is essential that we use the economic development board to provide this country with an adequate rate of economic growth. Then using the Atlantic development board, we can truly develop a sound industrial economic base and provide our people with a standard of living and equality of opportunity in line with people in the rest of Canada.

Atlantic Development Board all hope and expect it will be. From the debate on this legislation and from the lips of members from the Atlantic provinces must come ideas, enthusiasm and leadership. The legislation demands this type of approach; the board it will create demands it; and the members of that board must anticipate it. They must look to us to provide the initial ideas that could transform our area to one of health and vigour.
I was very pleased to see the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Forestry introduce this measure. He is a man who has provided outstanding leadership to our area throughout his life. He gave leadership to the present self-help approach to our problems on his election as premier of New Brunswick in 1952. Since that date we have seen the Atlantic premiers conference become an annual event of great significance. We have seen the establishment of the Atlantic provinces economic council, with the resultant benefits that have accrued to our area through their leadership. Now we see the minister guiding this legislation through the house. It is legislation which carries with it the hopes and aspirations of all in our area.
In order to assure the success of this board we must see to it that the ablest men in our area, regardless of their political affiliations, are appointed to it. We must see that they are presented at an early date with evidence that specific projects will have a long term beneficial effect on the economy of our area. We must hope and expect that the board will act quickly on those projects which have already had exhaustive investigations into their merits and demerits carried out. The board must move quickly in making the government aware of their recommendations and at that time we must move swiftly in seeing that the proper action is taken.
From a personal view, there are two specific projects which I consider merit early consideration by this house and by the board. The first is the Chignecto complex on which the minister has already made some comment. The second is the re-establishment of the Minas basin ferry service. The Chignecto complex does not demand the extensive investigation that might once have been required. The Chignecto canal committee has already had a comprehensive investigation carried out into the potential of the bay of Fundy tides, from an energy point of view. It is a study that demands the most intensive consideration and at the earliest date possible. With the development of this tidal power, one might well see the transformation of our area through a tremendous industrial expansion. This project has an

annual energy potential of 5| billion kilowatt hours. Estimates of mill rates run from 2.87 mills per kilowatt hour to 5.13 mills per kilowatt hour, depending on the interest rate and amortization. With this project we see the means by which we can accomplish the task before us. I might add that an integral part of this tidal development would be the construction of large thermal power plants. This would provide a much needed shot in the arm for the coal industry of our area. It is my view that we should expect an early report from the board on the feasibility of harnessing the tides. Certainly if a positive decision were brought down construction of the dam to harness the tides and construction of the thermal power plants should begin immediately.
The second project I feel could come before the board at an early date is the Minas basin ferry service. This is an important transportation facility that was available to the maritime provinces until 1940. At that time the ferry was removed from the area as a war measure and never returned. At the present time a great deal of information is available on the potential of this transportation link. The Stanfield government had a very exhaustive investigation carried out, and the only hindrance to its re-establishment has been the high cost of wharfage facilities. This link would provide a saving in mileage of as much as 115 miles to areas in the Annapolis valley and southwestern Nova Scotia. It is not difficult to imagine the great boost it would provide to the tourist industry, to agriculture and to our fisheries. There has been discussion of late on the possibility of obtaining a hovercraft. This craft would eliminate the heavy wharfage costs necessary for the ordinary type of facility if a scheduled service were to be provided.
There is another possibility associated with this transportation link between the Annapolis valley and Cumberland. It is the recommendation associated with the Chignecto complex that a dam be constructed to harness the waters of the Minas basin. This dam would be constructed where the ferry would operate. If the dam were recommended and could be used as a causeway as well, the need for the ferry service would be eliminated.
There are many projects related to every area of our economy which deserve consideration and action. It is up to us to see that they are brought to the board's attention. It is up to the board to see that they are dealt with swiftly. If the recommendation is positive, then the government must transform its recommendation into reality. If it is negative, we must immediately move on to another. There will be many projects submitted and

they will vary in their over-all effect. Certainly those with the greatest potential effect should be considered first. Let us work together to make this board what we feel it should be. Let us look forward to early results from our efforts.
Before resuming my seat, Mr. Chairman, I wish to pay tribute to Brigadier Michael Wardell. He has carried out a dedicated crusade to make the Atlantic development board a reality. His persistent guidance is exemplified by the fact that all four political parties during the last election campaign considered such a board essential as a cure for the ills of our area. He has been a visionary who, with the passage of this legislation, will see the initial step taken. Let us not fail in our quest to make the remainder of his dream as real as this initial step.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had not intended taking any part in the discussion of this resolution, but after listening to some of the government supporters speaking on it I thought I had better find out if they were talking about the same resolution that was being discussed by this committee. I listened to their eloquent exaggerations as to what this resolution will do, statements that this is the greatest piece of legislation ever passed in the interests of the maritimes, the statement that this is going to make the maritimers masters of their own destiny, and so on, and thought it might be a good thing if we just came back to the actual facts of this resolution before the debate is wound up.
Let me say, in the first place, that I think hon. members from all other parts of Canada will welcome the idea of having an Atlantic development board. I would like to compliment the minister who introduced the resolution. I know all hon. members of the house would want to say to him that neither he, the government nor anyone else need ever apologize for bringing in special legislation for this area of Canada. Because I think we agree with him when he says that this area deserves special consideration and demands special action. This is the case because the Atlantic provinces have had for many years a lower per capita income than the rest of Canada, a higher rate of unemployment than any other part of Canada-certainly higher than the national average-and they have had particular problems which have brought with them difficulties both social and economic.
I have been rather amused all day listening to the Liberal and Conservative members

each trying to lay the blame on the other party for the conditions in the Atlantic provinces. I certainly do not intend to get into this game of trying to prove that it is the Conservatives' fault or the Liberals' fault that conditions are as they are in the Atlantic provinces. All I want to say is that the conditions are there, that they are appalling, that both the old line parties which have governed Canada since 1867 must accept responsibility for this state of affairs, that there is not much use spending time in attaching blame; the problem now is to get on with the job of trying to improve the situation. It has been more than a matter of a lack of government policy.
We have had in Canada since 1867 national policies which have deliberately developed a great industrial heartland in central Canada. That policy, by means of transportation, tariffs and investment, has used western Canada and the Atlantic provinces to supply raw materials and fuel, and on the other hand has made them the market place for the products of central Canada. There is a price you have to pay for such a policy, and certainly the Atlantic provinces, and at certain times western Canada, have paid the price. Therefore, no one need apologize for saying that in those circumstances in addition to a national economic development board we need an Atlantic development board to pay particular attention to the problems of the Atlantic provinces.
I rose simply for the purpose of saying that I think supporters of the government would have been much fairer to this committee and to this country as well as to the eastern provinces of Canada if, instead of those purple passages about this being the magna carta of the Atlantic provinces they had simply said what was the truth, namely that they were going to set up a development board for the Atlantic provinces which would be an advisory board whose function apparently, would be to collect data, to look into the possibility of certain economic projects and to make recommendations. In other words, it would be a regional version of the national economic development board.
This resolution and the bill which will follow can be for the Atlantic provinces either invaluable or valueless, and what is done will depend entirely on the extent to which the recommendations of this board are implemented. Actually, much of its work has already been done by the Atlantic provinces economic council. APEC has produced reports on economic projects for the Atlantic provinces which are broad in scope and excellent in concept. So in actual fact

the board which it is now proposed to establish will not have to do very much work. Things like the Chignecto canal, the Fundy hydro power development and at least half a dozen cornerstone industries have been fully investigated by the Atlantic economic council. They have collected a wealth of data, and if all this board is going to do is mull over the same material its work will be a waste of time.
I personally would have preferred to see a department of government set up rather than an advisory board, because that is what this is. I would like to see a department charged for the present with the task of promoting economic development in the eastern provinces and raising the living standards there-a department with a minister, a deputy minister and staff. When the provinces had been brought up to the national standard, the department could be disbanded. Such a department which would have power and, above all, an allocation of funds and a clearly defined purpose in mind, might go far toward accomplishing this purpose. So let us not forget that this proposed board will be an advisory board and that if its recommendations do not receive any more attention than some of the recommendations of the various boards and commissions which have been set up during recent years, the resolution before us is not worth the paper it is printed on.
In the second place, the effectiveness of this board will depend on whether or not there is an Atlantic development fund set up from which the board can draw the funds necessary to implement its program. We do not need more economic surveys; we do not need more economic analyses; we do not need more paper plans. We have reached the point where money, and very large sums of money, are needed. The hon. member for Gloucester talked about a billion dollars over the next 10 years. A billion dollars over the next 10 years would not begin in my humble opinion to cope with the problem of economic development in the four Atlantic provinces.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: How much?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Much larger sums than that will be needed. As the hon. member for Red Deer pointed out, we are now spending $150 million a year on social welfare. I would say that a billion dollars over the next five years would be needed in the Atlantic provinces. If the expenditure of that money helps to provide full employment and takes people off the social welfare roll and off unemployment insurance, it will be the best investment the people of Canada ever made. So let us not begrudge the expenditure of money like
National Productivity Council Act this. When I hear members of the government side say "How much?" and "Where are you going to get it?" this makes me suspicious as to how much money will be behind this economic development board. If this is going to be just another board to cut out paper dolls and make coloured pictures and charts, I, for one, will be very disappointed. I want to tell the hon. member to my left that if, proportionately, the Atlantic provinces could get as much for industrial development as the province with which I was associated I think they would be very happy to see the government putting up that much money.
When the bill comes down, the sponsor of this resolution may be able to give us some information as to the machinery which will be set up for implementing the recommendations of this new board. He may be able to tell us what sums of money over what period of time will be available in an Atlantic economic development fund. I hope he will also be able to tell us whether or not the major economic groups in the Atlantic provinces will be represented on this board-whether business, labour, primary producers and consumers as well as the provincial governments will be represented, so that the board may be truly representative not only of the four provinces concerned but of the various economic outlooks involved.
We in our group will support this resolution but we will support it in the hope that all the good things which have been placed in the store window this afternoon will not prove to be just window dressing, but that when the bill comes down and when we go into the store there will be some goods on the shelf.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Flemming (Victoria-Carleion) thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. C-94, for the establishment of an Atlantic development board.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MEMBERSHIP, ETC.

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MEMBERSHIP, ETC.
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the National Productivity Council Act, to provide for the appointment of three additional members thereof and for the payment of certain expenses of such members, to provide further for the payment of all expenses of the council out of moneys appropriated by parliament for the purpose and to provide further for other related and incidental matters.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Paul in the chair.

National Productivity Council Act

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MEMBERSHIP, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the amendments to the National Productivity Council Act proposed by this resolution provide for the following changes. The membership of the council will be increased by three members, who will be additional representatives of the fields of industry and commerce, organized labour, agriculture and other primary industries. This will give the council a total membership of 28 persons. Provision will be made for the appointment of a vice chairman of the council who will assist the chairman and act in his absence. The staff of the council will be brought under the Government Employees Compensation Act. The council's expenses will be paid from moneys appropriated by parliament in the light of the council's programs instead of through a fixed annual amount established in the act as is at present the case.
The purpose of these amendments is to assist the council in carrying out this greatly expanded program. These activities have been developed in consultation with leaders of business, organized labour, education and provincial bodies. The new provisions should greatly strengthen the ability of the council to implement its new program, which takes on added importance in view of the proposed legislation to establish a national economic development board. The council and the development board will complement each other's activities, each lending support to the endeavours of the other. The activities of the development board will, however, emphasize and underline the need for effective measures on a wide front to help Canadian industry to be as competitive as possible. The productivity council will be concerned in large measure with this very important task.
Now, Mr. Chairman, during the past year and a half the council has planned and undertaken a very comprehensive program. All of these activities are intended to help Canadian businessmen to compete more effectively both in the home and in world markets. I should like briefly to mention some of the key features of this program, because I believe that businessmen, labour leaders and the general public should know more about the useful work being carried out by the council. In collaboration with the universities, the council is sponsoring courses on work study. In addition seminars, conferences, lectures, and discussion groups have been systematically organized to promote work study in industrial centres across Canada. The council is playing an important role in encouraging the development of improved management techniques, and the use of training and retraining programs. Extensive work is being undertaken in the field of human relations in industry. An examination of the

extent of industrial research in certain key industries is under way. Careful consideration is being given to ways of encouraging more research. Information on means of achieving greater productivity is being prepared by the council staff and made available to labour, management, educational institutions, and other groups interested in this vital task. In order to reach out to the grass roots of business, provincial and local productivity councils and committees have been organized across Canada.
The record, Mr. Chairman, I believe, is indeed impressive, and I would like to emphasize that I am mentioning only the highlights. The details are available for anyone who wishes to know them. I would encourage business and labour leaders to become familiar with them. Despite the tremendous job which the national productivity council is doing, the council cannot do it alone-it needs labour-management co-operation as well, and the help of Canadian universities is also most important. Labour and management are cooperating, and Canadian universities are also being very helpful.
The council has already forged some close links with our universities in its expanding program to foster and promote productivity. One of the strongest links is through its labour-management co-operation program. A series of national joint labour-management seminars is being sponsored by the council at Canadian universities. The first of these seminars was held last March, at Queen's university in Kingston. A second was held at Dalhousie University in Halifax in September. A third has already been planning at Saskatchewan university for next January, and plans are under way to hold a fourth in Quebec next spring. At these seminars, for the first time in Canada, top labour and management leaders are brought together to discuss their problems frankly with each other, away from the bargaining table, in a neutral university atmosphere. They talk together, eat together, and live together at the university. They learn to know each other better. Many of them, in fact, have been amazed to find that they are really not so far apart after all. This is a great contribution towards creating a better climate of labour-management relations by Canadian universities working with the national productivity council.
The success of these conferences can be attributed to the high calibre of the people attending and to the national stature and prominence of the speakers. The quality and usefulness of these conferences is typified by the program carried out at the Halifax meeting, and I think hon. members would be

interested in hearing something about it. At the plenary sessions of this meeting, the speakers included Professor W. Y. Smith, head of the department of economics and political science at the University of New Brunswick, and past chairman of the Atlantic provinces economic council, who spoke on the economic facts and their implications. Mr. Herbert H. Lank, president of Du Pont of Canada Limited, and Mr. William J. Smith, president of the Canadian brotherhood of railway, transport and general workers, discussed the subject of the problems of economic growth and productivity from the viewpoint of management and labour. Mr. Walter E. Duffett, dominion statistician, and Dr. S. A. Goldberg, assistant dominion statistician, gave talks on measuring productivity. Judge A. H. McKinnon of the province of Nova Scotia, chairman of the fact finding body on labour legislation, spoke on seeking a formula for industrial peace and collaboration. Also, during the plenary sessions, Mr. D. W. Ambridge, president of the Abitibi Power and Paper Company Limited, and Mr. J. A. D'Aoust, vice president and regional director of united papermakers and paperworkers, discussed labour-management co-operation at the industry and plant level.
One very important session at the Halifax meeting was the panel discussion on the findings of the national productivity council's mission to Europe on labour-management-government co-operation in European countries. Taking part in this discussion were Mr. R. V. Yohe, president of B. F. Goodrich Canada Limited; Mr. Jean Marchand, president, confederation of national trade unions; and Dr. G. V. Haythorne, deputy minister of labour, who is also a member of the national productivity council.
The announcement in the throne speech that a national economic development board would be established followed on the successful completion of the mission to Europe sponsored by the national productivity council. The members of the mission were drawn from the ranks of labour, management, education, and government. Organized labour was represented by Mr. William Dodge, executive vice president of the confederation of national trade unions. Mr. John D. Carroll, international representative and assistant to the Canadian vice president, international brotherhood of boilermakers, iron shipbuilders, blacksmiths, forgers and helpers; and Mr. Larry Sefton, director, district No. 6, united steelworkers of America. Management was represented by Mr. J. Herbert Smith, president of the Canadian General Electric Company Limited; Mr. Robert B. Yohe, president of B. F. Goodrich Canada Limited; and Mr. J. Claude Hebert, president, Transparent 27507-3-148
National Productivity Council Act Paper Products Ltd.; Dr. G. Edward Hall, president of the University of Western Ontario, represented educational institutions.
In each of the countries visited, the members of the mission held detailed discussions with leading representatives of national labour and management organizations; with government economic agencies; and with joint labour-management-government consultative bodies.
In sending this mission to Europe, the council believed that it was useful and desirable to have a better knowledge of the experience of other countries in undertaking economic activities intended to foster employment, and to achieve economic advancement. The mission visited Sweden, the Netherlands, West Germany, France, Belgium, and England, in investigating these matters. Following its return to Canada, its members prepared and published a very informative and useful report on European organizations, both governmental and private, which work toward economic expansion.
I regard the findings of this mission as being of the utmost importance. To a very large extent they confirm what this government has been attempting to do in fostering closer relations between labour, management and government. There is little doubt that labour, management and government co-operation in Europe has contributed greatly to the general prosperity in that area. It would be misleading, of course, to attribute the prosperity of Europe solely to this co-operation because many other factors have also contributed. Nevertheless, without close co-operation between the three key sectors of the economies of European countries, it is very doubtful that they would have achieved the amount of progress which has been possible.
While the policies and activities being implemented by the various countries visited by the mission showed differences, each had the same basic objective. In this regard the mission was impressed in each country with the spirit of co-operation which exists between labour, management and government, and the way in which they worked together in the national interest. There is little doubt that this co-operation has greatly contributed to the general prosperity of Europe. The determination of all key groups in each of these countries to achieve high levels of employment, economic growth, rising standards of living, and a healthy trading and balance of payments position, has made possible the recovery of Europe and the very impressive economic expansion in that area.
In view of the importance of having full labour participation in the productivity work, as evident by European experience, it is proposed to add to the council an additional

National Productivity Council Act person from organized labour. In this regard, we are very hopeful that the Canadian Labour Congress will soon see its way clear to participate in this important work. We would welcome having Mr. Claude Jodoin rejoin the council, or having other top calibre members of the congress sit upon the council. If Canada is to support a sustained rate of economic growth it is essential that we too achieve the spirit of co-operation which is so apparent in key countries of Europe. Labour, management and government must pull together, each making a contribution to common objectives which are in the interests of all Canadians.
There is a growing realization in Canada that Canadians must produce more in Canada, and must purchase more domestic goods. We could not continue indefinitely to have the deficit in our current balance of payments which has prevailed since the end of the last world war. If, however, we are to produce and sell more in Canada, Canadian products must be competitive with goods made in other countries. Canadian manufacturers must produce the types of goods which buyers find it is in their interest to purchase, those which are efficiently produced, and are of competitive quality, design and price. In achieving these objectives, the national productivity council has a major role to play. If the economy is to grow and expand, the council must initiate the types of activities and programs which will help Canadian producers to be competitive at home and in export markets. The council has made an excellent start in focusing the attention of labour and management on these activities, and in bringing them together to exert a co-operative effort. Now that the council's initial period of planning and organization is behind it, its activities are having beneficial effects on an increasing scale.
Realizing the vital role which it has to play in stimulating Canada's growth, the council has been preparing its program for the future. Additional labour-management seminars are being planned in co-operation with the universities. Steps are being taken to organize labour-management forums on a systematic basis. The program of training courses in work study will be expanded, so that this valuable instruction will be available at universities in various regions of Canada. More work is being initiated with a view to encouraging greater industrial research. As the provincial and area councils and committees become increasingly better organized, systematic programs of material will be fed out to them to be used as the basis for local productivity activities. Studies will be undertaken of important activities in the fields of

economics and the humanities which have a direct bearing on productivity.
The program is both vital and ambitious, and I feel sure that every Canadian will support it. I hope that it will receive the wholehearted endorsement and support of this House of Commons, so that the excellent work which was started a year and a half ago may proceed for the benefit of the country as a whole.

Now, I shall not go through all the other paragraphs in the report of this mission other than to point out that this council has indicated to the government in the report the need for planning. It has also recommended and advised the government that something must be done about the serious gap between management, labour and government consultation and co-operation in connection with providing Canada with the kind of plan which is necessary to bring us out of our economic doldrum. This government has not indicated that it intends to do anything about these recommendations under either the National Productivity Council Act or the economic development board.
I should like to point out a couple of other important subjects which I think should be dealt with, and the first is the question of overlapping. I believe that this is becoming increasingly serious, but I do not believe any spokesman for the government has indicated any constructive proposal which would clearly define the responsibilities of all these boards. The terms of reference of the national economic development board, as set out by the Minister of Finance, indicate that it plans to make proposals that cut across the whole range of financial and monetary policy and make constructive recommendations of a long range nature to the government. Almost identical terms of reference are set out for the national productivity council, at least the way the national productivity council itself interprets those terms of reference. This national productivity council has given notice to this government it intends to go into that very area during the forthcoming year. This afternoon we heard about the Atlantic development board which is presumably going into identical studies as the two other boards that have been set up, except that the work of this board will apply to a particular region. We have the national research council whose terms of reference closely approach the terms

of reference of all three boards. We have two programs under the defence research board. We have the Vocational Training Assistance Act under the Minister of Labour and the terms of reference of that legislation come well within those of the national productivity council and of these boards.
Presumably, if one listens to the comments coming from spokesmen for the government, all these bodies are to operate independently. Hon. members make general statements to the effect that it is hoped they will complement each other. However, they do not advise the Canadian public or the members of this house in a detailed way as to how all these various programs and boards plan to integrate their activities. There are so many boards now that I have even omitted one. As I look at the Minister of Labour, I recall he is recommending we establish a manpower adjustment board under the new legislation he plans to introduce. I believe the terms of reference of this body would fall within the terms of reference of not only the national economic development board but of this national productivity council.
I believe the government has an obligation to explain how they plan to avoid the collapse of this whole program for these boards in one hopeless mess of confusion which will bring further discredit to this country and which will probably mean our legislative program is again the laughing stock of the world, as has happened in connection with so many of the proposals of this government. When these various measures are discussed in the committee, the government should show in a detailed fashion how all the activities of these boards are to be integrated. This should be shown to the satisfaction of the personnel of the boards themselves and to the satisfaction of the Canadian people, so that the people will realize some constructive proposals will issue forth.
The Canadian public are not going to be satisfied with just a barebones explanation offered by this government for setting up a multiplicity of boards. The Canadian people and the members of this house want to know in a concrete way how the government plans these boards should operate so they will be co-operating. I think probably the most serious omission from the minister's speech when he introduced this amendment to the National Productivity Council Act was the omission of the word "planning". The productivity council dealt with this thoroughly, but the minister did not choose to mention it, did not choose to mention that he hoped the goals of this council would be the same as the goals of similar councils in western Europe and in other democratic nations that

have adopted these councils in the past. There should be a detailed plan of the economic goals for Canada that would be worked out by this council.
Apparently the government does not want that. Apparently the government is staying clear of that. If that be the case, then any concrete advantages that the efforts of this council may render the Canadian people are almost negligible because that is the whole purpose of the activities of this productivity council. In conclusion, I would say that the minister's comments indicate that the government has not dealt with the two main serious flaws in this legislation. This is the thing that has bothered the national productivity council all along. I refer to the terms of reference. Mr. Claude Jodoin resigned over that and, as I pointed out, the members of the council are not satisfied, as is indicated in the annual report. They want the terms of reference broadened so they can go into the economic measures necessary to increase productivity in a more comprehensive fashion. The government has not dealt with Mr. Jodoin's objection relating to the manner of representation, the manner of appointment. Until the minister is prepared to deal with all these problems, all we can say is this is just another board this government has set up to indicate that they plan to do something for the Canadian economy in the cheapest way possible, without going to work and developing long range policies of a concrete nature which are so badly needed.

Mr. Chairman, one of the lessons I learned out of my African experience relates to a condition caused by an organism known as taenia solium. If one dose would not take care of it, take a half dozen. This evening, I could not help but think that is just what is happening here in this house. Certainly we have been witnessing a great proliferation of government boards. It was interesting, however, to hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce speak about what a board has accomplished rather than to hear reference to what it is hoped a board will do.
I believe one board which has been set up by the government which has amply justified its existence is the national productivity council. I believe that the outline of some of the activities which have been carried on with a very meagre budget further confirms this conviction. The problem comes back to mind again: If this is what the national productivity council has done and is going to do, what in the world is going to be left for the national economic development board to do? Obviously they are going to overlap in many, many places. However, it is a matter of some encouragement to note the remarks of the
National Productivity Council Act minister, that there is going to be an overlapping of the membership structure of these boards. I trust that if this is going to be the pattern of the government it will soon mean the complete integration of the two boards. Certainly this is the only way either of them is going to be able to function effectively without getting in the other's way. Perhaps the greatest danger of overlapping of responsibilities is the fact that too often one board nullifies the potential objectives of the other. However, Mr. Chairman, I trust that with the appointment of these three additional members the way is being laid for these objectives to be achieved.
I believe it is our responsibility to give complete support to this resolution. I note with some satisfaction that the three additional members represent three very important aspects of our economy. I think the key to proper planning is not simply the laying down of some master plan from on top, but making it possible for people-this includes industry, labour and all aspects of organized activity and society-to co-operate and work with each other. We very often hear hon. members speak about the advantages of planning in Sweden, the Netherlands, West Germany or some other European countries. I do not think this has been accomplished because they have some super, master plan; it is simply because they have been able to get management and labour to co-operate with each other and with government in such a way as to enable them to make the progress which they obviously have made. They have done this simply by working out these problems in the very way the minister indicated some of the activities of the national productivity council have been carried on during the past year; that is, legitimate, grass roots planning. That is a different thing, though, than planning by a few sitting up at the top.
I think another very commendable aspect that has been brought to our attention this evening is that the work of the national productivity council is not going to be dependant upon a fixed budget passed on to them as their operating financial base. Any money invested in an organization such as the national productivity council as it performs its legitimate function is certainly the best kind of investment the government can make, and I think the suggestion that has been made will remove that bottleneck from the program and activities of the N.P.C. I believe this is good. The minister briefly outlined this evening some of the key features of the national productivity council. Again, I see a very definite overlapping with the summarized terms of reference, at least, of the national economic development board. I think all these points the minister covered are good. I was

National Productivity Council Act particularly impressed with the report of the European work study group. However, none of these things is of any use unless it actually produces the action that will reach through to the objectives that are being talked about.
Thus, Mr. Chairman, just briefly stating our thinking in regard to this particular resolution, I would again draw to the attention of the committee the fact that we have several obvious problems as they relate to the objectives of the national productivity council and the national economic development board. We are the greatest importing nation on earth in that our per capita imports are nearly triple those of our nearest competitor in this respect. I think what we must do is this. The government must give responsible assistance in solving this problem. We must produce here in Canada many of those things which today we are importing from abroad. This will never be done in a period of austerity. If there is not capital, on one hand, available to do this-and this is a very critical problem this winter; it affects the question of unemployment and the desired growth rate which we want to see for our economy-then we cannot solve the problem. It is absolutely essential that easier credit be available. On the other hand there must be those incentives -this again comes back to our tax problems -that will encourage our people to produce those things which in too great quantities are imported today. Again, Mr. Chairman, I mention an illustration to which I think I referred a few weeks ago. A senior trade official from Japan who is in this country at the present time told me that he was not interested in importing textiles into this country; he was far more interested in importing heavy, modern equipment which would bring our own textile factories up to the standards they ought to have, in order that we can produce our own textiles.
Then, unless we can increase the effective demand of our home market, any increase in productivity will be nullified. Again, I would seriously say to the hon. members of the committee that unless we can make our own financial system work in such a way that it puts into the hands of our people the effective ability to use what they themselves produce, what is going to be the use of increasing our productivity at all? Herein lies one of the basic problems that we face. The government must give the help that is necessary in this regard, not through welfare but through a financial policy that will meet our needs today; not a financial policy that met our needs 50 or 100 years ago. We live in an age of potential plenty; this is an age of abundance. Unless we gear our policies, whether they refer to taxation, monetary reform or ;any other aspect of our economy, to this age


of abundance we are simply going from one problem to another and any number of boards will not solve the problem.
There is another point, Mr. Chairman, and I think this comes within the terms of reference of the national productivity council. The productivity which is surplus to our economy and to the legitimate needs of our own country must find its way into the hands of those people elsewhere in the world who do not have the abundance that is ours. But this, again, is part of the function and purpose of the national productivity council and I am convinced that it is synonymous with the responsibilities which we would attach to the national economic development board. Thus I believe that the resolution which has been placed before us is commendable and is deserving of our support, provided it does work towards solving these aspects of our problems to which I have just referred.

The minister's approach to this reminds me of a problem I encountered when I was trying to write a study a few years ago on football and its appeal to crowds. I sent to the United States and picked up a Ph.D thesis on the whole relationship of football and crowds. It was a long, carefully written thing, beautifully documented, and the summary came down to this-that in relation to football and crowds the football teams are not really important; it is the cheerleaders who really make things go.
